lessons.title: Crisis Theory and the Nursing Role in Crisis Intervention
lessons.lay_summary: A crisis is a temporary state of disequilibrium where usual coping mechanisms fail. Nurses are often the first clinical contact and have a critical role in stabilisation.

content.intro: Crisis intervention is a short-term, goal-directed therapeutic approach aimed at restoring the individual to at least their pre-crisis level of functioning. Gerald Caplan's crisis theory (1961) and Lindemann's grief work form the theoretical basis. Roberts' Seven-Stage Crisis Intervention Model provides a practical nursing framework.

sections.title: Roberts' Seven-Stage Crisis Intervention Model
sections.body: Stage 1: Assess lethality — immediate safety assessment for suicidal/homicidal ideation and means. Stage 2: Establish rapport — non-judgmental presence, empathy, active listening. Stage 3: Identify the problem — what precipitated this crisis? (precipitating event). Stage 4: Deal with feelings — validate and explore emotional response. Stage 5: Explore alternatives — what has worked before? What resources are available? Stage 6: Develop an action plan — concrete, achievable steps, including safety planning if needed. Stage 7: Follow-up — schedule a follow-up contact or referral. The model is flexible — not always linear, but all stages must be addressed.

sections.title: Maturational vs Situational Crisis
sections.body: Maturational crises arise from normal developmental transitions that temporarily overwhelm coping: adolescence and identity formation, marriage, parenthood, retirement, death of a spouse. These are predictable and anticipatory guidance can mitigate impact. Situational crises are unexpected, external events: sudden illness, job loss, divorce, accidents, natural disasters, assault. Adventitious crises = large-scale disasters (pandemics, mass casualty events). Nursing response differs: maturational crises may benefit from normalisation and psychoeducation; situational crises require immediate practical support and safety assessment.

sections.title: Principles of Trauma-Informed Crisis Nursing
sections.body: SAMHSA's six principles: Safety (physical and emotional); Trustworthiness and transparency; Peer support; Collaboration and mutuality; Empowerment and choice; Cultural, historical, and gender sensitivity. Practical application: explain all actions before performing them; give choices wherever possible; do not use physical holds unnecessarily; avoid judgmental language about past behaviour; involve the patient in safety planning rather than imposing it. Avoid re-traumatisation: asking detailed questions about trauma history during acute crisis is contraindicated.

content.clinical_pearl: The strongest predictor of a successful crisis intervention is the quality of the therapeutic alliance established in the first five minutes. Introduce yourself, sit at the patient's level, use their preferred name, and demonstrate that you have time — even if you don't feel like you do.
key_points: Roberts' 7 stages: Lethality → Rapport → Problem → Feelings → Alternatives → Plan → Follow-up
Maturational = developmental transitions; situational = unexpected external events
Trauma-informed care: safety, transparency, empowerment, cultural sensitivity
Do NOT take a detailed trauma history during acute crisis — focus on stabilisation
Therapeutic alliance in the first 5 minutes is the strongest predictor of success
references: Roberts AR. Bossiere KJ. Crisis intervention handbook, 4th ed. Oxford University Press, 2015
SAMHSA. National Guidelines for Behavioral Health Crisis Care. 2020
SAMHSA. SAMHSA's Concept of Trauma and Guidance for a Trauma-Informed Approach. HHS Publication, 2014

lessons.title: Suicide Risk Assessment and Safety Planning
lessons.lay_summary: Suicide is a leading cause of preventable death. Every nurse — not just psychiatric nurses — must be able to assess suicide risk and initiate a safety plan.

content.intro: Suicide risk assessment is a core nursing competency across all specialties. The WHO estimates 700,000 suicide deaths annually globally. Many people who die by suicide had contact with a healthcare professional in the weeks before their death. The Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) is the validated, evidence-based tool endorsed by the FDA, Joint Commission, and WHO.

sections.title: The Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS)
sections.body: The C-SSRS assesses ideation intensity and behaviour separately. Ideation: 1 = Passive wish to be dead ('I wish I were dead'). 2 = Non-specific active ideation ('I want to kill myself' without plan). 3 = Active ideation with method (no plan or intent). 4 = Active ideation with plan. 5 = Active ideation with intent to act. Behaviour (lifetime/recent): preparatory actions, aborted attempts, interrupted attempts, actual attempts. High-acuity indicators: suicidal ideation type 4-5, recent attempt (last 3 months), specific plan, access to lethal means (especially firearms), male sex, older age, hopelessness (Beck Hopelessness Scale), impulsivity, intoxication, social isolation.

sections.title: Asking About Suicide: Overcoming Barriers
sections.body: Common myth: asking about suicide 'plants the idea'. Evidence: this is false. Direct, compassionate questioning does NOT increase suicide risk and often provides relief ('Someone finally asked'). Recommended approach: 'Sometimes when people are going through difficult times, they have thoughts of hurting themselves or ending their life. Is that something you've been experiencing?' Follow up: 'Have you thought about how you would do it?' and 'Have you taken any steps to prepare?' Document exact responses, not paraphrases. If patient denies but has high risk indicators — trust clinical judgement over verbal denial.

sections.title: Safety Planning (Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention)
sections.body: The safety plan is a collaborative written document — not a 'no-suicide contract' (which lacks evidence and may deter honest disclosure). Six components: 1. Warning signs of an impending crisis (specific to this patient). 2. Internal coping strategies (distraction, self-soothing — what has helped before?). 3. Social contacts who can distract (people to call, places to go). 4. People to ask for help (friends, family who know about suicidal thoughts). 5. Professional and crisis contacts (psychiatrist, crisis line — e.g. 988 in USA, Samaritans 116 123 in UK). 6. Means restriction — remove/secure access to lethal means, especially firearms and stockpiled medications. Review and update at each contact.

sections.title: Means Restriction Counselling
sections.body: Access to lethal means is the single most important modifiable risk factor for suicide completion. Most suicides involve impulsive decisions made during a short window of crisis — if the means are not immediately available, the crisis may pass. Firearms: account for ~50% of US suicide deaths. Ask directly about firearms in the home; recommend temporary removal or secure storage (gun lock, third-party storage). Medications: patients at risk should be prescribed limited quantities; involve family/carers in monitoring and securing medications. The nurse's role is to facilitate this conversation with the patient and family — not to make judgements about firearm ownership.

content.clinical_pearl: Hopelessness, not depression severity, is the strongest predictor of suicide. The Beck Hopelessness Scale (BHS) correlates better with suicide completion than PHQ-9. A depressed patient who believes things can get better is at lower risk than one who says 'Nothing will ever change.'
key_points: C-SSRS ideation 1-5: passive wish → active with intent; all level 4-5 require urgent intervention
Asking about suicide does NOT increase risk — it often provides relief
Safety plan ≠ no-suicide contract; must include means restriction
Hopelessness (BHS) is a stronger predictor of completion than depression severity
Firearms account for ~50% of suicide deaths; means restriction is the most impactful intervention
references: Columbia University Medical Center. Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS). 2008
Stanley B, Brown GK. Safety Planning Intervention. Cognitive Behavioral Practices, 2012;19:256-263
Mann JJ et al. Suicide prevention strategies. JAMA 2005;294(16):2064-2074

lessons.title: Substance Use Disorders: Recognition and Nursing Care
lessons.lay_summary: Substance use disorders affect millions worldwide. Nurses encounter patients with these disorders across all settings — not just psychiatric units. Stigma is a major barrier to care.

content.intro: Substance use disorder (SUD) is defined by the DSM-5 as a problematic pattern of substance use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, manifesting as 2+ of 11 criteria within a 12-month period. SUD exists on a severity spectrum (mild: 2-3 criteria, moderate: 4-5, severe: 6+). The chronic brain disease model — not moral failing — underpins evidence-based treatment.

sections.title: DSM-5 SUD Criteria (11 criteria across 4 domains)
sections.body: Impaired control: 1. Taking more than intended / longer than intended. 2. Persistent desire or unsuccessful attempts to cut down. 3. Great deal of time obtaining/using/recovering. 4. Craving. Social impairment: 5. Failure to fulfil major role obligations. 6. Continued use despite persistent social/interpersonal problems. 7. Important activities given up. Risky use: 8. Recurrent use in hazardous situations. 9. Continued use despite physical or psychological harm. Pharmacological: 10. Tolerance (needing more to achieve same effect). 11. Withdrawal (characteristic syndrome or use to relieve/avoid withdrawal). Note: tolerance and withdrawal alone do not constitute SUD in patients taking medications as prescribed (e.g. opioids for pain, benzodiazepines for anxiety).

sections.title: CAGE and AUDIT Screening Tools
sections.body: CAGE (4 questions): Cut down ('Have you ever felt you should cut down?'), Annoyed ('Have people criticised your drinking?'), Guilty ('Have you felt guilty about your drinking?'), Eye-opener ('Have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning to steady your nerves?'). Score ≥2 = clinically significant; sensitivity 43-94% for alcohol dependence. AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test): 10 questions; score 0-40. Recommended by WHO. Score 8-15 = hazardous use (brief intervention); 16-19 = harmful use (brief counselling + monitoring); ≥20 = probable dependence (referral). DAST-10 equivalent for drugs.

sections.title: Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) for Opioid Use Disorder
sections.body: MAT is the evidence-based gold standard for opioid use disorder (OUD). Methadone: full opioid agonist; dispensed daily from licensed clinic; reduces cravings and prevents withdrawal; high overdose risk if diverted. Buprenorphine (Suboxone = buprenorphine/naloxone): partial agonist; ceiling effect reduces overdose risk; can be prescribed in office-based settings. Naltrexone (Vivitrol): opioid antagonist; blocks euphoria; must be opioid-free for 7-10 days before initiation or will precipitate withdrawal; IM injection monthly. Nursing role: administer medications, monitor for diversion, provide psychoeducation, support adherence, assess for continued use.

sections.title: Harm Reduction Approach
sections.body: Harm reduction accepts that abstinence is not always immediately achievable and focuses on reducing the harms associated with substance use. Evidence-based interventions: needle and syringe programmes (reduce HIV, Hepatitis C transmission); naloxone distribution (opioid overdose reversal — every nurse should know how to administer nasal naloxone); supervised injection facilities; fentanyl test strips. Nurses should be familiar with naloxone: dose for opioid overdose = 0.4-2 mg IV/IM/SC/intranasal; repeat every 2-3 minutes if no response; naloxone half-life is shorter than most opioids — patient may re-narcotise after apparent recovery; observe for minimum 4 hours post-administration.

content.clinical_pearl: Language matters in SUD care. 'Person with substance use disorder' reduces stigma compared to 'addict' or 'drug abuser'. Studies show healthcare providers who use stigmatising language provide lower quality care. Use person-first, non-judgmental language — it directly impacts clinical outcomes.
key_points: DSM-5 SUD: 2+ of 11 criteria in 12 months; mild (2-3), moderate (4-5), severe (6+)
CAGE ≥2 and AUDIT ≥8 are positive screens for problematic alcohol use
MAT for OUD: methadone (full agonist), buprenorphine (partial agonist), naltrexone (antagonist)
Naloxone: 0.4-2 mg IV/IM/IN; repeat every 2-3 min; observe ≥4 hours post-dose
Person-first language ('person with SUD', not 'addict') improves care quality
references: WHO. The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT). WHO, 2001
SAMHSA. Medications for Opioid Use Disorder. Treatment Improvement Protocol (TIP) 63, 2021
Ashford RD et al. Stigma and addiction: how language affects clinical outcomes. J Addict Medicine, 2019

lessons.title: Alcohol and Opioid Withdrawal: Clinical Management
lessons.lay_summary: Alcohol withdrawal is potentially fatal. Opioid withdrawal is very uncomfortable but rarely life-threatening. Nurses must recognise and escalate withdrawal syndromes promptly.

content.intro: Withdrawal syndromes occur when a physiologically dependent person abruptly reduces or stops substance use. The severity and timeline differ markedly between substances. The Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA-Ar) for alcohol and COWS for opioids are the validated nursing tools for monitoring withdrawal severity and guiding treatment.

sections.title: Alcohol Withdrawal: Timeline and Clinical Features
sections.body: Timeline (from last drink): 6-12h: autonomic hyperactivity — tremor, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety. 12-24h: hallucinations (alcoholic hallucinosis) — visual, tactile ('formication' = sensation of insects on skin), usually with intact orientation. 24-48h: seizures (withdrawal seizures — generalised tonic-clonic; risk is higher with prior withdrawal seizures). 24-72h (peak): delirium tremens (DTs) — confusion, agitation, severe autonomic instability; 5-15% mortality if untreated. Mortality risk factors: concurrent illness, prior DTs, prolonged heavy use, older age.

sections.title: CIWA-Ar: Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol
sections.body: CIWA-Ar assesses 10 items: Nausea/vomiting, Tremor, Paroxysmal sweats, Anxiety, Agitation, Tactile disturbances, Visual disturbances, Auditory disturbances, Headache, Orientation. Each scored 0-7 (except orientation 0-4). Maximum score: 67. Score <10: mild (monitor q1-4h). Score 10-15: moderate (consider pharmacotherapy). Score ≥15: severe (pharmacotherapy essential, consider ICU). Treatment: IV/PO benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, or lorazepam) — symptom-triggered dosing using CIWA is more effective and uses less medication than fixed-schedule dosing. Also: thiamine 100 mg IV before any dextrose (Wernicke's prevention), magnesium repletion.

sections.title: Wernicke's Encephalopathy Prevention
sections.body: Wernicke's encephalopathy results from acute thiamine (B1) deficiency — common in alcohol dependence. Classic triad (all three present in <20% of cases): Confusion/delirium, Ophthalmoplegia (eye movement abnormalities — lateral gaze palsy, nystagmus), Ataxia. If untreated → Korsakoff's psychosis (permanent anterograde amnesia with confabulation). Critical nursing action: give IV thiamine BEFORE any IV dextrose/glucose in any patient with suspected alcohol dependence presenting to hospital. Glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's in a thiamine-depleted patient. Thiamine dose: 200-500 mg IV TDS × 3-5 days for treatment; 100 mg IV/IM for prophylaxis.

sections.title: Opioid Withdrawal: COWS Assessment
sections.body: Opioid withdrawal is not life-threatening in healthy adults but is intensely uncomfortable. Timeline (short-acting opioids — heroin, oxycodone): onset 8-24h after last use, peak 36-72h, resolution 5-7 days. Symptoms: yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, piloerection ('goose flesh'), sweating, anxiety, restlessness, myalgia, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dilated pupils, tachycardia. COWS (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale): assesses 11 signs, score 5-12 mild, 13-24 moderate, 25-36 moderately severe, >36 severe. Treatment: buprenorphine (gold standard — reduces withdrawal and craving; initiate when COWS ≥8-12 and patient in mild-moderate withdrawal), methadone, clonidine (symptom relief — autonomic symptoms only), loperamide (diarrhoea), NSAIDs (myalgia).

content.clinical_pearl: Never give IV dextrose to a patient with suspected alcohol dependence without thiamine first. The mnemonic: 'Banana bag before bag' (Banana bag = IV thiamine + folate + multivitamin). This is one of the most important and most forgotten nursing actions in acute alcohol presentations.
key_points: Alcohol withdrawal timeline: 6-12h tremor → 12-24h hallucinations → 24-48h seizures → 24-72h DTs
CIWA-Ar ≥15: severe withdrawal — pharmacotherapy mandatory, consider ICU
Wernicke's triad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia — give thiamine BEFORE glucose
COWS ≥8: initiate buprenorphine; must be in mild-moderate withdrawal before first dose
Opioid withdrawal: not fatal in healthy adults; alcohol withdrawal can kill
references: Sullivan JT et al. Assessment of alcohol withdrawal: The CIWA-Ar. Br J Addiction 1989;84:1353-1357
WHO. Clinical guidelines for withdrawal management and treatment of drug dependence in closed settings. 2009
Weaver MF. Prescription sedative misuse and abuse. Yale J Biology Medicine 2015;88(3):247-256

lessons.title: Recognising and Responding to Abuse
lessons.lay_summary: Abuse — domestic, child, elder — is a public health crisis. Nurses are mandated reporters in most jurisdictions and are often the first professional a victim discloses to.

content.intro: Abuse encompasses physical, emotional/psychological, sexual, and financial harm, as well as neglect. Healthcare settings — emergency departments, antenatal clinics, paediatric wards — are key points of detection. Nurses must know their jurisdiction's mandatory reporting obligations and how to safely enquire about abuse without endangering the victim.

sections.title: Domestic Violence and Abuse (DVA): SAFE Questioning
sections.body: DVA affects ~1 in 4 women and 1 in 6 men globally. It occurs across all socioeconomic, ethnic, and age groups. Warning signs: unexplained injuries (especially in distribution inconsistent with mechanism), delay between injury and seeking care, partner who attends and speaks for the patient, patient who is fearful, overly vigilant, or deferential. SAFE framework: Stress/Safety ('Do you feel safe at home?'), Afraid/Abused ('Have you been hit, kicked, or hurt by anyone?'), Friends/Family ('Do you have people you can turn to?'), Emergency plan ('If things escalate, do you have somewhere safe to go?'). Always ask in private — never in front of the suspected abuser.

sections.title: Child Abuse: Recognition and Mandatory Reporting
sections.body: Types: physical (unexplained bruising — especially in non-mobile infants, ear/face/torso distribution, patterned injuries, multiple ages of bruising), sexual (genital injury, sexualised behaviour, STI in a child), emotional (failure to thrive, fearful behaviour), neglect (poor hygiene, hunger, untreated medical conditions). Highly suspicious: bruising in non-mobile infants (<6 months), fractures inconsistent with developmental stage, retinal haemorrhages (shaken baby), multiple fractures at different healing stages. Mandatory reporting: in most jurisdictions, all healthcare professionals must report suspected child abuse to child protective services. Your role is to report reasonable suspicion — not to investigate. Document factually: direct quotes, objective observations, body map of injuries.

sections.title: Elder Abuse
sections.body: Elder abuse affects 1 in 6 people aged 60+ globally (WHO). Types: physical, psychological/emotional, sexual, financial/material, neglect (active or passive), abandonment. Risk factors: cognitive impairment (dementia), social isolation, dependence on caregiver, prior history of violence. Warning signs: poor hygiene, malnutrition, unexplained injuries, fear of caregiver, unexplained financial transactions, caregiver who refuses to leave the patient alone, caregiver who speaks for the patient. The Elder Assessment Instrument (EAI) can assist structured assessment. Reporting obligations vary by jurisdiction but most mandate report if the elder lacks capacity to protect themselves.

content.clinical_pearl: Safety planning with DVA victims is complex. Never advise a victim to 'just leave' — the period of leaving is the most dangerous time for homicide risk. Collaborate with the patient on a safety plan: emergency bag packed, trusted contact, local shelter numbers. Your role is to offer resources and believe — not to rescue.
key_points: SAFE questioning: Stress/Safety, Afraid/Abused, Friends/Family, Emergency plan; always in private
Bruising in non-mobile infants is highly suspicious — mandatory report
You report reasonable suspicion — you do not investigate child abuse
Elder abuse: 1 in 6 over-60s affected; cognitive impairment and isolation are risk factors
Leaving DVA is the highest-risk period; safety planning > 'just leave'
references: NICE. Guideline NG76: Domestic violence and abuse. NICE, 2014 updated 2023
WHO. Global status report on violence prevention. 2014
Pillemer K et al. Elder abuse: global situation, risk factors and prevention strategies. Gerontologist 2016;56(Suppl 2)

flashcards.question: Roberts' 7 stages of crisis intervention?
flashcards.answer: 1.Lethality assessment, 2.Rapport, 3.Identify problem, 4.Deal with feelings, 5.Explore alternatives, 6.Action plan, 7.Follow-up

flashcards.question: Alcohol withdrawal DTs: when and mortality?
flashcards.answer: 24-72h after last drink; 5-15% mortality if untreated. Preceded by tremor (6-12h), hallucinations (12-24h), seizures (24-48h).

flashcards.question: Why must thiamine precede IV dextrose in alcohol dependence?
flashcards.answer: Glucose metabolism requires thiamine. Giving glucose to a thiamine-depleted patient precipitates Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia → Korsakoff's if untreated).

flashcards.question: C-SSRS ideation levels 4 and 5?
flashcards.answer: Level 4: active ideation with specific plan. Level 5: active ideation with intent to act. Both require immediate intervention.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse in the ED is caring for a woman with multiple bruises in various stages of healing. The patient's partner stays very close and answers questions on her behalf. The nurse's PRIORITY action is:

options.A: Treat the injuries and discharge without confrontation
options.B: Ask the partner to wait outside and speak privately with the patient
options.C: Document suspected abuse and continue the visit normally
options.D: Confront the partner about the bruises

mcq_questions.explanation: Separating the potential victim from the suspected abuser is the priority — it allows private, safe disclosure. Abusers commonly control the narrative during healthcare visits. After separation, use validated screening (HITS or SAFE questions). Mandatory reporting varies by state for adult IPV but is required for child/elder abuse. Confronting the abuser can escalate danger.

mcq_questions.question: A patient in alcohol withdrawal presents with HR 120, BP 160/100, temperature 38.2°C, and generalized tremors. Their CIWA-Ar score is 18. Which treatment is MOST appropriate?
mcq_questions.explanation: CIWA-Ar ≥10 indicates moderate-severe withdrawal requiring benzodiazepines. IV/IM lorazepam (or diazepam) is the first-line treatment — GABA-A agonists prevent seizures and DTs. Haloperidol lowers seizure threshold and worsens withdrawal. Naltrexone is for maintenance, not acute withdrawal. Thiamine is adjunct (given before dextrose) but does not treat withdrawal itself.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse using crisis intervention for a patient threatening self-harm should FIRST:

options.A: Assess the patient's usual coping mechanisms
options.B: Establish rapport and ensure immediate safety

mcq_questions.explanation: Roberts' 7-Stage Crisis Intervention Model begins with: (1) assess lethality and immediate danger, (2) establish rapport. Safety is the foundation of all crisis intervention — without it, no therapeutic work can proceed. Coping assessment and history are important but secondary. Family contact may be appropriate but requires patient consent and comes after stabilization.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is assessing a 4-year-old child who presents with multiple bruises on the buttocks and inner thighs in various stages of healing. The parent's explanation is inconsistent with the injury pattern. The nurse MUST:

options.A: Document and report suspected child abuse to child protective services
options.B: Ask the child directly if they were hurt by their parent
options.C: Confront the parent about the inconsistency
options.D: Wait for more evidence before reporting

mcq_questions.explanation: Nurses are mandated reporters. Suspected child abuse MUST be reported regardless of certainty — the threshold is reasonable suspicion, not proof. Injuries in protected areas (buttocks, inner thighs) with inconsistent explanation are highly concerning. Mandated reporters are protected from liability for good-faith reports. Direct forensic questioning of the child should be done by trained investigators to avoid contaminating testimony.

mcq_questions.question: Which assessment finding in an opioid-dependent patient who received naloxone 30 minutes ago is MOST concerning?

options.C: Return of pinpoint pupils and RR 8/min
options.D: Requesting water and complaining of headache

mcq_questions.explanation: Naloxone has a shorter half-life (30–90 min) than most opioids. Renarcotization — return of opioid toxidrome (miosis, respiratory depression) after naloxone wears off — is the primary danger. RR 8 with pinpoint pupils after naloxone indicates renarcotization requiring repeat dosing and continuous monitoring. Mild agitation is expected (opioid withdrawal precipitation); requesting water is benign.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse performs a CAGE assessment. A patient answers 'yes' to 3 of 4 questions. This result suggests:
mcq_questions.explanation: CAGE: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener. ≥2 positive answers has 60–95% sensitivity for alcohol use disorder — requires further evaluation and intervention. 3-4 positives strongly suggests dependence. CAGE screens specifically for alcohol, not other substances. A positive screen initiates brief intervention, referral, and medical assessment for withdrawal risk.

mcq_questions.question: A pregnant patient in her third trimester discloses she has been using heroin daily. The MOST appropriate initial intervention is:

options.A: Immediate referral to detoxification (cold turkey withdrawal)
options.B: Methadone or buprenorphine maintenance therapy with obstetric co-management

mcq_questions.explanation: SAMHSA guidelines strongly recommend medication-assisted treatment (methadone or buprenorphine) in pregnancy — NOT abrupt withdrawal. Opioid withdrawal in pregnancy risks preterm labour, placental abruption, and fetal death. Methadone/buprenorphine stabilizes the fetus. Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) is expected and manageable. Naltrexone is contraindicated in active opioid use (precipitates withdrawal).

mcq_questions.question: An elderly patient presents with confusion, unexplained weight loss, poor hygiene, and fearful body language toward the adult son who is the caregiver. This presentation is MOST consistent with:
mcq_questions.explanation: Multiple red flags for elder abuse: weight loss (neglect), poor hygiene (neglect), fearful affect toward caregiver (possible physical/psychological abuse), and confusion that may be from malnutrition or fear. Elder abuse affects 1 in 10 elderly Americans. Assessment tools include the Elder Abuse Suspicion Index (EASI). Mandatory reporting applies in all US states for elder abuse in care settings.

mcq_questions.question: During a Motivational Interviewing session, a patient states: 'I know I should stop drinking, but I'm not sure I'm ready.' The BEST response using MI principles is:

options.A: "You need to stop drinking now — it will kill you"
options.B: "What would need to be different for you to feel ready?"
options.C: "You've already tried before and failed — what makes this time different?"

mcq_questions.explanation: Motivational Interviewing uses open-ended questions, affirmations, reflective listening, and summaries (OARS). The patient is in the contemplation stage (Prochaska's TTM). Exploring what would build readiness honors autonomy and evokes the patient's own motivation (internal vs. external). Confrontation ('you'll die') creates reactance. MI is non-confrontational and collaborative.

mcq_questions.question: A patient arrives in the ED after a suicide attempt by overdose. After medical stabilization, the psychiatry team recommends discharge. The nurse's PRIORITY before discharge is:

options.A: Provide a list of crisis hotline numbers
options.B: Ensure a safety plan is developed and the patient can verbalize it
options.C: Contact the patient's employer about the absence
options.D: Arrange a follow-up appointment in 30 days

mcq_questions.explanation: A safety plan (Stanley-Brown model) is evidence-based crisis planning: warning signs, coping strategies, social contacts, means restriction, and professional contacts. The patient must be able to verbalize and demonstrate understanding. Means counselling (removing firearms, medications) is critical. Follow-up within 24–72 hours, not 30 days. Hotline numbers alone are insufficient after a serious attempt.

mcq_questions.question: Which finding in a patient with cocaine intoxication requires IMMEDIATE intervention?

options.C: Chest pain with ST-segment elevation on ECG

mcq_questions.explanation: Cocaine causes coronary vasospasm and thrombosis leading to myocardial infarction — the most common cause of cocaine-related death. ST-elevation indicates STEMI requiring immediate cath lab activation. Note: nitroglycerin and calcium-channel blockers are used over beta-blockers (beta-blockers can worsen cocaine-induced vasospasm via unopposed alpha activity). Aspirin and benzodiazepines (for hypertension/agitation) are first-line.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse documents suspected child abuse. The parent threatens the nurse with a lawsuit if a report is made. The nurse's BEST response is:

options.A: Delay the report until consulting hospital legal counsel
options.B: Proceed with the mandatory report — nurses are legally protected for good-faith reports
options.C: Document the parent's threat and wait for supervisor approval
options.D: Transfer care to a physician to make the report

mcq_questions.explanation: All 50 US states grant immunity from civil and criminal liability for mandated reporters who make good-faith reports. Failing to report is a crime — penalties include license revocation and prosecution. The duty to report is the nurse's individual legal obligation and cannot be transferred. Threats from parents do not suspend mandated reporting requirements.

mcq_questions.question: Which nursing intervention BEST supports recovery for a patient with substance use disorder being discharged to the community?

options.A: Instruct the patient to avoid all social contact for 6 months
options.B: Connect the patient with peer support, MAT continuation, and community recovery services
options.C: Provide a list of inpatient detox programs only
options.D: Advise the patient to rely solely on willpower

mcq_questions.explanation: Recovery is sustained by a continuum of care: medication-assisted treatment (MAT — buprenorphine/methadone for opioids, naltrexone for alcohol), peer support specialists, 12-step or SMART Recovery meetings, case management, and housing stability. Isolation increases relapse risk. Willpower-only approaches have the lowest evidence base. The SAMHSA 8 Dimensions of Wellness framework guides holistic recovery.
